# Schema: how this library is compiled

This repository is a **deliverables library built as an LLM wiki** — a knowledge base
built on compilation rather than retrieval. The raw sources are the deliverables a
firm has produced for its clients (credit card spend analyses, cash flow projections,
philanthropic giving summaries, estate reviews, performance summaries, internal
methodology memos). You are the compiler. This file is the language spec you compile
against.

```
raw/          the deliverables   (immutable — humans add them, you never edit)
   │
   │  ingest / compile           ← you
   ▼
wiki/         compiled pages     (you own this entirely: clients, services, topics)
   │
   │  lint                       ← tools/wiki.py, deterministic
   ▼
answers       runtime            (query reads wiki/, not raw/)
```

The point of the pattern: what the firm knows across its deliverables is **compiled
once and kept current**, not re-derived from the documents on every question. A query
that has to re-read `raw/` is a cache miss and means the library is incomplete — fix
the library, don't just answer.

**Everything in `raw/` and `wiki/` is synthetic.** The clients, the company names and
every figure were invented for this demonstration. The previous demo corpus (the LLM
wiki pattern compiled from its own literature) is kept under `examples/llm-wiki-pattern/`.

## Hard rules

1. **Never edit `raw/`.** A deliverable is the record of what the firm told a client.
   If a deliverable is wrong, note the error on the page that cites it; if a later
   deliverable revises it, that is a supersession (rule 5), not an edit.
2. **Every claim carries a citation.** Any sentence asserting a fact — a figure, a
   recommendation, a finding — cites the deliverable it came from as `[^source-id]`.
   Synthesis you performed yourself is marked `[^synthesis]` — that is an honest
   citation, not an escape hatch.
3. **Cite ids that exist.** Every `[^id]` must match a `source_id` in `raw/`, and must
   also appear in the page's frontmatter `sources:` list. `wiki lint` enforces this.
4. **Contradictions are content, not errors.** When two deliverables disagree about the
   same thing — the same charge categorised two ways, a projection's assumption
   contradicted by a later measurement — do not average them and do not silently pick a
   winner. Mark the page `status: contested` and write a `## Contradictions` section
   naming which deliverable claims what. Lint fails a `contested` page that lacks one.
5. **Supersede, don't delete.** When a revised deliverable overturns an earlier one,
   keep the old conclusion on the page, mark it superseded, link the revision, and date
   it. The firm's earlier advice cannot be audited if it disappears.
6. **No numeric confidence scores.** Use the categorical `status` field. A score
   assembled from source count and recency has no units and no calibration.
7. **Never invent a client, a figure or a deliverable.** If the library cannot answer,
   say so and name which deliverable is missing.

## Page types

| type | one page per | what it compiles |
|---|---|---|
| `client` | client household or entity | everything the firm has told that client, across deliverables; open items; superseded advice |
| `service` | kind of deliverable | what it covers, the method, who has one, what it reliably finds, how it has held up |
| `topic` | recurring theme | a finding or piece of advice that recurs across clients or deliverables |
| `question` | — | what the deliverables raise and do not settle, each with the deliverable that would settle it |
| `overview` | — | `synthesis` (start here), `index` (generated), `log` (append-only) |

## Page frontmatter

```yaml
---
title: Kessler family
type: client              # client | service | topic | question | overview
status: established       # established | contested | provisional | superseded
updated: 2026-09-21       # the date YOU last compiled this page
sources:                  # every source_id cited in the body
  - kessler-card-analysis-2025
  - kessler-cash-flow-2026-05
---
```

`status` values:

| value | meaning |
|---|---|
| `established` | multiple deliverables agree, or one authoritative deliverable and no dissent |
| `contested` | deliverables disagree — **requires** a `## Contradictions` section |
| `provisional` | one deliverable, unreplicated, or your own synthesis |
| `superseded` | overturned; must link forward to the page that replaced it |

## Deliverable frontmatter (`raw/`)

```yaml
---
source_id: kessler-cash-flow-2026-05         # client-deliverable-period; the citation key
title: "Cash flow projection 2026–2035 — Kessler family trust (May 2026 revision)"
author: Planning team
client: Kessler family
deliverable: Cash flow projection
period: 2026-2035
published: 2026-05-20                         # delivered on
added: 2026-05-20                             # added to the library; drives staleness
kind: deliverable
capture: synthetic                            # synthetic | verbatim | summary
---
```

File name: `raw/<added>-<source_id>.md`.

## Link conventions

- **Page links:** `[[clients/kessler]]` — a path under `wiki/` without the `.md`. Lint
  resolves every one and fails on breaks.
- **Citations:** `[^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]` — a `source_id` from `raw/`.
- Aim for 3+ outbound links per page. A page nothing links to is an orphan, and lint
  reports it — knowledge that cannot be reached is not knowledge.

## The four operations

### ingest — add a deliverable

1. Human drops a file in `raw/` with the provenance frontmatter above.
2. Read it fully. Do not skim. Figures matter; carry them over exactly.
3. Find every existing page it touches — `grep`, and read `wiki/index.md`. A deliverable
   touches **at least** its client page, its service page and every topic page whose
   theme it bears on. Expect to update several pages, not to write one new one. A new
   client or service page is the exception, created only when none exists.
4. For each affected page: fold in the new claim, add the citation, update `sources:`
   and `updated:`, and ask explicitly whether the deliverable *contradicts* or
   *supersedes* what is there. If it does, apply rule 4 or rule 5.
5. Append to `wiki/log.md`.
6. Run `python3 tools/wiki.py lint` and fix what it reports.

### compile — rebuild stale pages

`wiki lint` reports pages whose cited deliverables are newer than the page itself —
the same dependency check `make` does. Recompile those pages against their current
deliverables.

### query — answer from the library

1. Search `wiki/`, not `raw/`. Read the pages, follow the links.
2. Answer with citations, carried through from the pages. Citations are deliverable
   ids, so the reader can open the deliverable itself. For "which clients" and "what
   have we done" questions, answer with a list or table naming the deliverable behind
   each row.
3. If the library could not answer, that is a **compiler bug**. Either the deliverable
   was never ingested, or it was ingested badly. Say so, then fix it.
4. If the answer contained genuine new synthesis, **file it back as a page.** Insight
   that stays in the chat log is lost work.
5. Append the query and its verdict to `wiki/log.md`.

### lint — check the build

`python3 tools/wiki.py lint`. Deterministic, no API key, no LLM. It checks the
mechanical invariants only — broken links, uncited claims, missing contradiction
sections, stale pages, uningested deliverables. It cannot tell you whether a page is
*true*, or whether a figure was carried over correctly. That judgement is yours, and it
is the part that does not automate.

## What this schema deliberately does not do

- **No epistemic filter.** Nothing checks that a figure on a page matches the
  deliverable. A well-formed citation to a real deliverable can still sit next to a
  wrong number. `status` is a weak proxy, applied by the same model that wrote the page.
- **No decay.** Pages do not age out. A client page compiled once and never revisited
  looks identical to one that survived four deliverables.
- **Human gate on writes.** Ingest is run deliberately, not on a hook, because
  event-driven auto-ingest assumes reliable LLMs and corrupts silently when that
  assumption breaks.

See [[questions/open-questions]].

# Credit card spend analysis — Abernathy-Ruiz household, CY2025

> **Synthetic demo data.** The household, the amounts and the card programmes are
> invented for this demonstration. Nothing here describes a real client.

**Prepared for:** Dana Abernathy and Marco Ruiz
**Scope:** all charges on the household's three personal credit cards, 1 Jan – 31 Dec 2025
**Method:** statement download, merchant categorisation under the firm's spend
categorisation standard v2, manual review of every charge over $1,000.

## Headline

Total card spend for 2025 was **$187,400** across three cards, up 9% on 2024. Travel
is the largest category and dining grew fastest.

| category | 2025 spend | share | vs 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Travel | $58,100 | 31% | +6% |
| Household & retail | $41,200 | 22% | +4% |
| Dining | $26,200 | 14% | **+22%** |
| Children & education | $16,900 | 9% | +11% |
| Subscriptions | $11,200 | 6% | +18% |
| Charitable | $9,400 | 5% | +40% |
| Other | $24,400 | 13% | +2% |
| **Total** | **$187,400** | 100% | +9% |

## Findings

1. **Subscriptions.** 47 recurring charges were identified. Nine are unused or
   duplicated (two streaming services with overlapping catalogues, a gym membership
   with no visits since March, three software tools tied to a closed side project,
   and three magazine renewals). Cancelling them saves **$2,340 a year**.
2. **Dining** rose 22% year on year, driven by weekday lunches near Marco's hospital
   and a standing Friday reservation. This is the only category growing faster than
   household income.
3. **Charitable** spend of $9,400 includes a **$4,500 table at the Harbor Arts Gala**
   (October) and $4,900 of other charges to registered charities. Under standard v2
   charity-related charges are categorised as charitable in full.
4. **Rewards.** 412,000 points are unredeemed across the three programmes, worth
   roughly **$6,200** at the firm's default valuation of 1.5 cents per point. Two of the
   programmes devalue points annually.
5. **Card structure.** Three cards with overlapping benefits cost $1,245 in annual
   fees; two would cover every benefit actually used.

## Recommendations

- Consolidate from three cards to two (drop the card whose lounge access duplicates
  another's), saving $550 in annual fees.
- Cancel the nine flagged subscriptions ($2,340 a year).
- Redeem the 412,000 points against 2026 travel before the next devaluation.
- Set a 2026 travel budget of $50,000 and review it in the mid-year check-in.
- Confirm the deductible portion of the gala table with the philanthropy team; the
  card analysis records the charge, not its tax treatment.

# Cash flow projection 2026–2030 — Abernathy-Ruiz household

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented household and figures, for demonstration only.

**Prepared for:** Dana Abernathy and Marco Ruiz
**Horizon:** five years, 2026–2030, annual resolution
**Inputs:** 2025 tax return, compensation statements, the 2025 credit card spend
analysis, mortgage and insurance schedules.

## Base case

| line | 2026 |
|---|---|
| Salaries (Dana, Marco) | $480,000 |
| RSU vesting (Dana; grant fully vests March 2028) | $132,000 |
| **Gross income** | **$612,000** |
| Income and payroll taxes | ($186,000) |
| Card spend (carried from the 2025 card analysis) | ($187,400) |
| Non-card spend: mortgage $62,000, insurance $14,000, childcare and tuition $31,000, utilities and other $24,000 | ($131,000) |
| **Total spend** | **($318,400)** |
| **Savings capacity** | **$107,600** |

Assumptions: discretionary card spend held **flat at the 2025 level** of $187,400;
non-card spend inflates at 3% a year; salaries grow 3%; RSU vesting continues at
$132,000 a year until the March 2028 cliff and then stops.

## Scenarios

- **Independent school for both children from 2027** adds $64,000 a year. Savings
  capacity falls to about **$43,600**.
- **RSU cliff (2028).** After March 2028 the $132,000 of annual vesting ends. With
  the school scenario in place, savings capacity turns **negative (about −$88,000)
  from 2029** unless spend adjusts or a new equity grant is made.
- **Base case only.** Without the school change, capacity stays positive through
  2030 even after the RSU cliff, at about $20,000 a year from 2029.

## Recommendations

1. Maximise both 401(k) plans ($47,000 combined in 2026).
2. Fund the two 529 plans at $30,000 a year in total while RSU income lasts.
3. Direct a further $30,000 a year to the taxable account.
4. Hold six months of total spend (about $160,000) in cash.
5. Revisit the plan at the RSU cliff, and earlier if the school decision is made.
6. The flat-spend assumption is the most fragile input. Card spend grew 9% in 2025;
   if that continues, capacity falls by roughly $17,000 a year, compounding.

# Philanthropic giving summary, tax year 2025 — Abernathy-Ruiz household

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented household, charities and figures.

## Giving in 2025

| vehicle | amount | deductible |
|---|---|---|
| Contribution to the Community Foundation donor-advised fund (cash) | $15,000 | $15,000 |
| Direct gifts to registered charities | $4,300 | $4,300 |
| Harbor Arts Gala table (October) | $4,500 | $2,900 |
| **Total** | **$23,800** | **$22,200** |

Giving was **3.9% of adjusted gross income** (AGI of about $612,000).

Only **$2,900 of the $4,500 gala table is deductible**: the charity's acknowledgement
values the dinner and entertainment received at $1,600, and that portion is a
purchase, not a gift.

**Note on the card analysis.** The 2025 credit card spend analysis reports $9,400 of
"charitable" spend, categorising the full $4,500 gala table as charitable and
including $600 of raffle tickets and merchandise bought at charity events. This summary
counts $4,300 of direct gifts, because raffle tickets and merchandise are purchases.
The two deliverables describe the same charges under different rules and the
difference is worth settling in the firm's categorisation standard.

## Tax position

Itemised deductions for 2025 were about $34,000 against a standard deduction of about
$31,000, so the giving produced very little incremental tax benefit.

## Recommendations

1. **Bunch two years of giving.** Contribute the planned 2026 and 2027 giving
   (about $40,000) to the donor-advised fund in 2026, itemise in 2026, and take the
   standard deduction in 2027. Grants to charities can continue on the usual schedule.
2. **Give appreciated RSU shares, not cash.** Shares held for more than a year can be
   contributed at fair market value with no capital gains tax on the appreciation.
   Dana's 2024 vest lots qualify from mid-2025.
3. Ask event organisers for the goods-and-services value in writing at purchase, so
   the deductible portion is known before year end.
4. Keep the gala table in the household's giving total for planning purposes, but
   record it separately from gifts.

# Spend categorisation standard, version 3

> **Synthetic demo data.** An invented internal memo for a fictional firm.

**Applies to:** every credit card spend analysis produced from Q3 2026. Analyses
produced under version 2 are **not restated**.

## Why a new version

Version 2 categorised any charge to a registered charity as *charitable*. The
philanthropy team then had to re-examine those charges to work out which were gifts and
which were purchases (gala tables, auction items, raffle tickets, memberships with
benefits). The two teams' numbers for the same client disagreed, and clients noticed.

## Categories

| category | definition |
|---|---|
| Travel | transport, lodging, travel insurance, foreign transaction fees |
| Dining | restaurants, delivery, bars |
| Household & retail | groceries, home goods, clothing, personal care |
| Home & garden | contractors, maintenance, garden, furniture over $500 |
| Children & education | tuition, childcare, activities, school supplies |
| Medical & pharmacy | providers, pharmacies, equipment |
| Subscriptions | recurring charges of the same amount in three or more consecutive months |
| **Events & memberships** (new) | charity galas and tables, auction purchases, raffle tickets, club and museum memberships |
| Charitable | gifts to registered charities where **no goods or services** are received |
| Other | everything else |

## Rules

1. **Charity-related purchases go to Events & memberships**, not Charitable and not
   Dining, at the full amount charged. Flag them `possible-charitable`. The
   philanthropy team determines the deductible portion in the giving summary; the card
   analysis never states tax treatment.
2. A **subscription is "unused"** when there is no correlated activity for 90 days and
   the client confirms it on review. Report the annualised saving from cancellation.
3. **Rewards points** are valued at 1.5 cents per point unless the programme publishes a
   different redemption value.
4. Every charge over $1,000 is reviewed by hand.
5. Where an analysis for a prior period used version 2, say so in the method note and
   do not compare Charitable or Dining totals across versions without adjustment.

# Credit card spend analysis — Kessler family, CY2025

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family and figures.

**Prepared for:** Ilse and Tomas Kessler
**Scope:** two personal credit cards, 1 Jan – 31 Dec 2025
**Method:** statement download, categorisation under standard v2, manual review of
charges over $1,000.

## Headline

Total card spend was **$96,300**. Travel dominates because of a six-week trip to
Europe in May and June.

| category | 2025 spend | share |
|---|---|---|
| Travel | $42,400 | 44% |
| Home & garden | $17,300 | 18% |
| Dining | $11,600 | 12% |
| Medical & pharmacy | $10,600 | 11% |
| Grandchildren (gifts, activities) | $5,800 | 6% |
| Subscriptions | $3,100 | 3% |
| Other | $5,500 | 6% |
| **Total** | **$96,300** | 100% |

## Findings

1. The Europe trip accounts for **$28,100** of travel. It was paid on a card with a
   3% foreign transaction fee and no primary travel insurance, costing about $840 in
   fees and leaving a cancelled rail segment uncovered.
2. **Subscriptions.** 14 recurring charges, of which four are unused (a second
   streaming service, a roadside-assistance plan duplicated by the auto insurer, and
   two app subscriptions). Cancelling them saves **$860 a year**.
3. **Disputed charges.** Two fraudulent charges totalling **$1,140** were identified
   in August, disputed, and recovered in full.
4. **Rewards.** 180,000 points are unredeemed, worth about **$2,700** at 1.5 cents
   per point.
5. Medical spend is stable and largely reimbursable; $2,200 of eligible receipts had
   not been submitted to the supplemental plan.

## Recommendations

- Move travel spend to a card with no foreign transaction fee and primary travel
  insurance before the 2026 trips.
- Cancel the four unused subscriptions ($860 a year).
- Submit the $2,200 of outstanding medical receipts.
- Redeem the 180,000 points against 2026 travel.

# Cash flow projection 2026–2035 — Kessler family trust, November 2025 edition

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family and figures.
>
> **Superseded** by the May 2026 revision, which reflects the lake house purchase.
> Kept in the library as the record of what the firm advised in November 2025.

**Prepared for:** Ilse (68) and Tomas (72) Kessler, trustees
**Horizon:** ten years, 2026–2035

## Position

| item | value |
|---|---|
| Kessler Family Trust, taxable portfolio | $8,400,000 |
| Tomas's IRA | $1,100,000 |
| **Total investable** | **$9,500,000** |
| Annual spending | $260,000 |
| Social Security (both) | $58,000 |
| **Net portfolio draw** | **$202,000 (2.1% of investable)** |

## Projection

- The net draw of 2.1% is well under the firm's 3.5% sustainability ceiling.
- Required minimum distributions from Tomas's IRA begin in 2027, when he turns 73,
  and are projected at about $42,000 in the first year. They exceed the IRA's share of
  spending, so part of each RMD will be reinvested in the taxable account.
- Under the base return assumption (5% nominal, 2.5% inflation) the portfolio's real
  value **rises in every scenario tested**, including a 20% equity drawdown in 2027.
- **No major purchases are assumed.** The trustees indicated none were planned.

## Conclusion

The plan is sustainable indefinitely at current spending. There is room for either
increased spending of up to $70,000 a year or accelerated gifting to the grandchildren
without breaching the ceiling.

## Recommendations

1. Keep spending at or below $330,000 a year (the level at which the draw reaches
   3.5%).
2. Begin Roth conversions from Tomas's IRA in 2026 to reduce future RMDs.
3. Revisit if spending, health, or a large purchase changes the picture.

# Cash flow projection 2026–2035 — Kessler family trust, May 2026 revision

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family and figures.

**Supersedes** the November 2025 edition. That edition assumed no major purchases; in
March 2026 the trustees agreed to buy a lake house for **$1,900,000**, closing in
July 2026. This revision reflects the purchase and its carrying costs.

## What changed

| item | November 2025 | May 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Major purchases | none | lake house, $1,900,000, July 2026 |
| Annual spending | $260,000 | **$298,000** (adds $38,000 of carrying costs: tax, insurance, upkeep) |
| Taxable portfolio after funding | $8,400,000 | **$7,400,000** after a $1,000,000 liquidation |
| Net portfolio draw | $202,000 (2.1%) | **$295,000 (3.5%)** including $55,000 of interest |
| Verdict | sustainable indefinitely | **at the ceiling; sustainable only with the funding structure below** |

## Recommended funding structure

Paying the full $1,900,000 from the taxable portfolio would realise an estimated
**$210,000 of capital gains** (about $50,000 of tax) and push the draw above 4%.
Instead:

1. **Liquidate $1,000,000** from the taxable portfolio, choosing the highest-basis
   lots to keep realised gains near the $210,000 estimate or below it.
2. **Borrow $900,000 on a pledged-asset line** secured by the trust portfolio, at about
   6.1%, costing roughly $55,000 a year in interest. Repay from RMDs and portfolio
   income over five to seven years rather than selling further appreciated positions.
3. Keep the **$1,000,000 in cash from June** so the closing does not depend on market
   conditions in July.

## Projection under the recommended structure

- Net draw of **3.5%** in 2026 and 2027, falling to about **3.0%** by 2029 as the line
  is repaid and RMDs (from 2027, about $42,000 in the first year) cover part of spend.
- The portfolio's real value is roughly flat through 2030, then rises. This is a
  materially weaker position than the November edition showed, and the
  "sustainable indefinitely" conclusion of that edition **no longer applies**.
- **Roth conversions** of about $150,000 a year in 2026 and 2027 remain attractive:
  the trustees are in a low bracket before RMDs begin, and conversions reduce the RMDs
  that would otherwise be forced later.

## Recommendations

1. Adopt the liquidate-plus-borrow structure above.
2. Hold spending other than the house at the 2025 level; the $70,000 of headroom the
   November edition identified is gone.
3. Proceed with Roth conversions in 2026 and 2027.
4. Review annually; a second property or a spending increase would breach the ceiling.

# Quarterly investment performance summary, Q2 2026 — Kessler family trust

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family and figures.

## Position at 30 June 2026

| item | value |
|---|---|
| Taxable portfolio | $7,600,000 |
| Cash held for the July closing | $1,000,000 (included above) |
| Tomas's IRA | $1,140,000 |
| Allocation (equity / fixed income / cash) | 52% / 41% / 7% |

## The lake house liquidation

In June the trust sold **$1,000,000** of taxable holdings to fund the July closing, as
recommended in the May cash flow revision. Using specific-lot identification to sell the
highest-basis positions first, **realised gains were $118,000**, against the
**$210,000 estimated** in the projection. The difference reflects lot selection, not a
change in the plan, and reduces the expected tax on the sale to about $28,000.

The $900,000 pledged-asset line was established in June and will be drawn at closing.

## Performance

| period | portfolio | blended benchmark | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026 | +1.4% | +1.9% | −0.5% |
| Year to date | +3.8% | +4.6% | −0.8% |

The shortfall is explained by two things: the $1,000,000 held in cash from June ahead
of closing (about −0.5% on the year), and an underweight to international equities that
rallied during the quarter (about −0.3%). Neither is a manager or security-selection
issue.

## Actions

- Cash drag ends at closing; no rebalancing is needed until the line begins to be
  repaid.
- Increase the international equity weight to the policy target of 15% in Q3.
- Roth conversion of $150,000 executed in June per the May plan.

# Estate and liquidity review, March 2026 — Okonkwo household

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family, company and figures. Larkspur Systems is a
> fictional company.

**Prepared for:** Chidi and Amara Okonkwo

## Position

| item | value |
|---|---|
| Net worth | $31,400,000 |
| Investable assets | $23,300,000 |
| of which Larkspur Systems shares (Chidi is a co-founder) | **$11,200,000 (48% of investable)**, cost basis $1,400,000 |
| Cash and short-term holdings | $1,900,000 |
| Annual spending | $1,600,000 |
| Okonkwo Family Foundation (separate) | $4,800,000 |

## Concentration

Nearly half of the family's investable assets are in one stock with a very low basis.
A 40% fall in Larkspur would remove about $4.5 million of net worth. Chidi is subject to
trading windows and to Section 16 reporting.

**Recommendation:** adopt a 10b5-1 plan selling **10% of the holding each year for four
years**, which keeps sales inside the company's rules and spreads the gain across tax
years. Use shares, not cash, for all charitable giving: a gift of appreciated stock held
more than a year is deductible at fair market value with no capital gains tax on the
appreciation, so every dollar given in shares reduces concentration at no tax cost.

## Liquidity

Cash and short-term holdings cover about **14 months of spending**. That is adequate,
but the household's spending has grown 12% a year for three years; if that continues
the buffer falls under 12 months by 2027. Hold the buffer at 12 to 18 months and top it
up from the 10b5-1 sales.

## Estate

- The couple has used $4,200,000 of its combined lifetime exemption.
- **GRAT:** fund a two-year grantor retained annuity trust with $3,000,000 of Larkspur
  shares. If the stock outperforms the hurdle rate, the excess passes to the children
  free of gift tax; if it does not, little is lost.
- **ILIT:** the existing $10,000,000 second-to-die policy should be moved into an
  irrevocable life insurance trust so the proceeds sit outside the taxable estate.
- **Foundation grants:** the foundation makes many small grants at a high
  administrative cost. Grants under $25,000 could be routed through the family's
  donor-advised fund instead.

## Actions

1. File the 10b5-1 plan before the next trading window.
2. Fund the GRAT in Q2 2026.
3. Establish the ILIT and transfer the policy.
4. Coordinate 2026 giving with the philanthropy team so it is made in Larkspur shares.

# Philanthropic giving summary, tax year 2025 — Okonkwo family and foundation

> **Synthetic demo data.** Invented family, foundation and figures.

## Family philanthropic activity, 2025

| vehicle | amount |
|---|---|
| Okonkwo Family Foundation grants (23 grantees) | $250,000 |
| Grants from the family's donor-advised fund | $110,000 |
| Direct gifts by the household (cash) | $52,000 |
| **Total philanthropic activity** | **$412,000** |

The **household's own giving** in 2025 was **$162,000**: the $110,000 of DAF grants was
funded by contributing **$110,000 of Larkspur Systems shares** to the donor-advised
fund, plus $52,000 of direct cash gifts. Household giving was **18% of adjusted gross
income** (AGI of about $900,000).

## Giving in shares

The Larkspur shares contributed had a cost basis of $14,000, so giving them rather than
selling them **avoided about $96,000 of capital gains**. Gifts of appreciated stock to
public charities and donor-advised funds are deductible up to 30% of AGI, leaving about
$270,000 of headroom in 2025. This is the approach recommended in the March 2026 estate
and liquidity review, and it should be the default for all of the family's giving.

## The foundation

- Grants of $250,000 represent a **5.2% payout** on foundation assets of $4,800,000,
  above the 5% minimum.
- Administrative costs were **$35,000, or 14% of grants**. The usual range for a
  foundation of this size is 5% to 8%. Most of the cost is the accounting and
  reporting burden of 23 separate grants, 16 of which were under $25,000.

## Recommendations

1. Make all household giving in Larkspur shares; the household has not used cash for
   gifts above $5,000 since 2024 and should stop doing so entirely.
2. Route grants under $25,000 through the donor-advised fund, leaving the foundation
   with about seven larger grants. Estimated saving: $20,000 a year in administration.
3. Set a 2026 giving budget in shares of $250,000 for the household, aligned with the
   10b5-1 sale schedule so concentration falls faster.
4. Consolidate the foundation's grantee list at the autumn board meeting.

# Abernathy-Ruiz household

Dana Abernathy and Marco Ruiz, two children aged 9 and 12 in 2026, combined gross income
of about $612,000 of which $132,000 is RSU vesting that ends in March 2028
[^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]. Three deliverables in the library: a 2025 credit card
spend analysis, a 2026–2030 cash flow projection, and a 2025 giving summary [^synthesis].

## What the firm has told them

**Spending.** 2025 card spend was $187,400 across three cards, up 9% on 2024, with
travel the largest category (31%) and dining growing fastest (+22%)
[^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]. Nine of 47 subscriptions were unused, worth
$2,340 a year, and 412,000 points (about $6,200) sat unredeemed
[^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]. See [[services/credit-card-spend-analysis]] and
[[topics/unused-subscriptions]].

**Cash flow.** Savings capacity is about $107,600 a year in the base case, falling to
about $43,600 if both children move to independent school from 2027, and turning
negative from 2029 once the RSU grant has fully vested unless spending adjusts
[^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]. The projection carries card spend forward flat at the
2025 level and names that as its most fragile assumption
[^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]. See [[services/cash-flow-projection]].

**Giving.** 2025 giving was $23,800, or 3.9% of AGI, of which $22,200 was deductible,
and produced almost no tax benefit because itemised deductions barely exceeded the
standard deduction [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025]. The recommendation is to bunch
2026 and 2027 giving into the donor-advised fund in 2026 and to give appreciated RSU
shares rather than cash [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025]. See
[[services/philanthropic-giving-summary]] and [[topics/giving-appreciated-shares]].

## Open items across deliverables

- The card analysis and the giving summary categorise the same $4,500 gala table
  differently; the disagreement is recorded at [[topics/spend-categorisation]]
  [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025].
- The cash flow's flat-spend assumption has not yet been checked against 2026 card

- The household's income depends heavily on a single equity grant until 2028
  [^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]. See [[topics/concentrated-stock-positions]].

## Recommendations still open

Consolidate to two cards, cancel the nine subscriptions, redeem points against 2026
travel [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]; fund 401(k)s and 529s and hold six months
of spend in cash [^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]; bunch giving in 2026
[^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025].

# Kessler family

Ilse (68) and Tomas (72) Kessler, retired, trustees of the Kessler Family Trust, with
investable assets of about $9.5 million at the end of 2025 [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11].
Four deliverables in the library: a 2025 card analysis, two editions of a ten-year cash
flow projection, and the Q2 2026 performance summary [^synthesis].

## The lake house

In March 2026 the trustees decided to buy a lake house for $1,900,000, closing in July
2026, which invalidated the November 2025 projection's assumption of no major purchases
[^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. The firm's advice was to liquidate $1,000,000 from the
taxable portfolio and borrow $900,000 on a pledged-asset line rather than sell
$1,900,000 of appreciated holdings [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. The June sale realised
$118,000 of gains against the $210,000 estimated, because the highest-basis lots were
sold first [^kessler-performance-2026q2]. See [[topics/funding-a-large-purchase]].

## Sustainability, then and now

| | November 2025 edition | May 2026 revision |
|---|---|---|
| annual spending | $260,000 [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11] | $298,000 [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05] |
| net portfolio draw | 2.1% [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11] | 3.5%, at the ceiling [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05] |
| verdict | sustainable indefinitely [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11] | sustainable only with the liquidate-and-borrow structure [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05] |

**Superseded claim (2026-05-20).** The November 2025 edition concluded the plan was
sustainable indefinitely with $70,000 a year of spending headroom
[^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11]. The May 2026 revision withdraws both conclusions: the
headroom is gone and the draw sits at the 3.5% ceiling [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05].
The earlier edition is kept in the library as the record of what was advised at the
time [^synthesis]. See [[services/cash-flow-projection]].

## Spending and cards

2025 card spend was $96,300, 44% of it travel, dominated by a $28,100 six-week trip to
Europe paid on a card with a 3% foreign transaction fee and no primary travel insurance
[^kessler-card-analysis-2025]. Four of 14 subscriptions were unused ($860 a year) and
two fraudulent charges totalling $1,140 were recovered [^kessler-card-analysis-2025].
See [[services/credit-card-spend-analysis]] and [[topics/unused-subscriptions]].

## Investments

The taxable portfolio stood at $7.6 million at 30 June 2026 including the $1,000,000
held for closing, returning +3.8% year to date against +4.6% for the benchmark; the gap
is cash drag ahead of closing and an underweight to international equities
[^kessler-performance-2026q2]. A $150,000 Roth conversion was executed in June, the
first of two planned before RMDs begin in 2027 [^kessler-performance-2026q2]
[^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. See [[services/investment-performance-summary]].

## Concentration is the organising problem

Every recommendation in both deliverables reduces the Larkspur position: a 10b5-1 plan

Things the deliverables raise and the library cannot yet answer. Each names the

## 1. Does the flat-spend assumption hold?

its most fragile input, noting that 9% annual growth would cut savings capacity by

[^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. Only the last is confirmed by a later deliverable

from, and no other retired household is in the library to compare
[^synthesis]. *Settled by:* a methodology memo for cash flow projections, like the one

# Cash flow projection

A multi-year projection of income, tax, spending and savings capacity, built from tax
returns, compensation statements, the household's card analysis and fixed-cost
schedules, with named scenarios and a recommendation list
[^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026]. Three are in the library: one for the Abernathy-Ruiz
household and two editions for the Kessler family trust [^synthesis].

| [[clients/kessler]] | 2026–2035, May 2026 revision | net draw 3.5% after the lake house, at the ceiling [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05] |

## Conventions the projections share

- **A sustainability ceiling of 3.5%** net portfolio draw for retired households
  [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11] [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05].
- **Card spend is carried in from the card analysis** and, in the working-household
  case, held flat, which the projection itself names as its most fragile assumption
  [^abernathy-ruiz-cash-flow-2026].
- **Base returns of 5% nominal and 2.5% inflation** for the retired case
  [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11].
- **Revisions supersede rather than amend.** The May 2026 Kessler revision states
  that the November edition's conclusion no longer applies and keeps a
  side-by-side table of what changed [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05].

## How projections have held up

The one projection with a follow-up so far is the Kessler funding plan: the estimated
$210,000 of realised gains from a $1,000,000 liquidation came in at $118,000 because
the highest-basis lots were sold first, so the plan's tax cost was lower than projected
without any change to the plan [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]
[^kessler-performance-2026q2]. See [[topics/funding-a-large-purchase]] and
[[services/investment-performance-summary]].

No working-household projection has yet been checked against a later card analysis,
so whether the flat-spend assumption holds is an open question [^synthesis]. See
[[questions/open-questions]].

# Credit card spend analysis

An annual review of every charge on a household's personal cards: statements are
downloaded, merchants are categorised under the firm's spend categorisation standard,
and every charge over $1,000 is reviewed by hand [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]
[^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. Two are in the library, both for calendar
2025 and both produced under version 2 of the standard
[^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025] [^kessler-card-analysis-2025].

## What it reliably finds

- **Unused subscriptions**, in every analysis so far: nine of 47 for the
  Abernathy-Ruiz household ($2,340 a year) and four of 14 for the Kesslers ($860 a
  year) [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025] [^kessler-card-analysis-2025]. See

- **Unredeemed rewards**, valued at 1.5 cents a point: 412,000 points (about $6,200)
  and 180,000 points (about $2,700) respectively [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]
  [^kessler-card-analysis-2025] [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3].
- **Card structure problems**: overlapping annual fees for one household, and a
  travel-heavy household paying 3% foreign transaction fees with no primary travel
  insurance [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025] [^kessler-card-analysis-2025].
- **Fraud**: two charges totalling $1,140 recovered for the Kesslers
  [^kessler-card-analysis-2025].

## What it does not do

The analysis records charges, not their tax treatment; under version 2 it categorised
charity-related charges as charitable in full, which the giving summary then
re-examined and partly reclassified [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]
[^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025]. Version 3 of the standard moves such charges to
a new "events & memberships" category and forbids stating tax treatment in the card
analysis [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. The disagreement between the 2025
deliverables is recorded at [[topics/spend-categorisation]].

## Method changes to watch

Analyses from Q3 2026 use version 3, and charitable and dining totals cannot be
compared across versions without adjustment [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3].
Both 2025 analyses will need that adjustment when the 2026 editions arrive
[^synthesis]. Their spending totals feed directly into each household's
[[services/cash-flow-projection]].

A point-in-time review of net worth, concentration, cash runway and estate structure,
ending in an action list [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. One is in the library, for
the Okonkwo household in March 2026, so this page is provisional: it describes one
deliverable, not a pattern [^synthesis].

## The Okonkwo review

- **Concentration:** 48% of investable assets in Larkspur Systems shares at a
  $1.4 million basis; a 10b5-1 plan selling 10% a year for four years is recommended,
  with all charitable giving made in shares [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. See
  [[topics/concentrated-stock-positions]].
- **Liquidity:** about 14 months of spending in cash, to be held at 12 to 18 months and
  topped up from planned sales [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026].
- **Estate:** $4.2 million of exemption used; a two-year GRAT funded with $3 million of
  shares and an ILIT for the $10 million second-to-die policy
  [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026].
- **Foundation:** route grants under $25,000 through the donor-advised fund
  [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026].

## Follow-through

The giving summary produced three months later confirms the share-giving approach was
already in use in 2025 and quantifies the foundation problem the review pointed at:
administrative cost of 14% of grants, driven by 16 grants under $25,000
[^okonkwo-philanthropy-2025]. See [[services/philanthropic-giving-summary]] and
[[clients/okonkwo]].

A tax-year review of a household's giving by vehicle, with the deductible amount, the

Both summaries recommend giving appreciated shares rather than cash, and the Okonkwo

Two households in the library depend on a single company's stock, in different ways:
one holds it, the other is paid in it [^synthesis].

## Holding it: the Okonkwo family

Larkspur Systems shares are $11.2 million, 48% of investable assets, at a $1.4 million
basis, and a 40% fall would remove about $4.5 million of net worth
[^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. The firm's plan reduces the position through three
channels at once: a 10b5-1 plan selling 10% of the holding a year for four years, a
GRAT funded with $3 million of shares, and all charitable giving made in shares
[^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. The giving channel is already working: $110,000 of
shares went to the donor-advised fund in 2025, and the 2026 budget is $250,000 of
shares timed with the sale schedule [^okonkwo-philanthropy-2025]. See

vested shares rather than cash is a small additional way to diversify

# Funding a large purchase

The library has one worked case, followed from projection to execution: the Kessler
family's $1,900,000 lake house, closing July 2026 [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05].

## The choice

Paying the whole price from the taxable portfolio would have realised an estimated
$210,000 of gains and pushed the net draw above 4%, past the firm's 3.5% ceiling
[^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. The recommended structure was to liquidate $1,000,000,
selling the highest-basis lots, and borrow $900,000 on a pledged-asset line at about
6.1%, repaid from RMDs and portfolio income over five to seven years
[^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. Cash for the closing was to be raised in June so the
purchase did not depend on July markets [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05].

## What happened

The trust sold $1,000,000 in June using specific-lot identification and realised
$118,000 of gains, well under the estimate, cutting the expected tax to about $28,000;
the line was established in June for drawing at closing [^kessler-performance-2026q2].
The cost was about 0.5% of year-to-date return in cash drag
[^kessler-performance-2026q2].

## What it cost the plan

The purchase moved the household from a 2.1% net draw with $70,000 of spending headroom
to a 3.5% draw with none, and the earlier "sustainable indefinitely" verdict was
withdrawn [^kessler-cash-flow-2025-11] [^kessler-cash-flow-2026-05]. See
[[clients/kessler]], [[services/cash-flow-projection]] and
[[services/investment-performance-summary]].

# Giving appreciated shares

The firm's standing advice, repeated in three deliverables: give shares held for more
than a year rather than cash, because they are deductible at fair market value and the
appreciation is never taxed [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025]
[^okonkwo-philanthropy-2025] [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026].

## Evidence in the library

- **Okonkwo, 2025:** $110,000 of Larkspur shares with a $14,000 basis contributed to
  a donor-advised fund, avoiding about $96,000 of capital gains, with about $270,000
  of headroom left under the 30%-of-AGI limit [^okonkwo-philanthropy-2025].
- **Abernathy-Ruiz, recommended for 2026:** contribute 2024-vest RSU lots, which
  qualify as long-term from mid-2025, instead of the cash used in 2025
  [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025].

## Two jobs at once

For a concentrated holder the gift is also a diversification tool, since every dollar
given in shares reduces the position at no tax cost; the Okonkwo estate review makes
share-giving a rule for that reason [^okonkwo-estate-liquidity-2026]. For a household
whose giving barely clears the standard deduction, shares plus bunching two years of
gifts into a donor-advised fund in one year is what turns the giving into a deduction
at all [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025]. See [[topics/concentrated-stock-positions]],
[[services/philanthropic-giving-summary]], [[clients/okonkwo]] and
[[clients/abernathy-ruiz]].

# Spend categorisation

How a charge is categorised decides which deliverable's number a client sees, and two
deliverables in the library disagree about the same charges [^synthesis]. The case is
the Abernathy-Ruiz household's 2025 giving: a $4,500 table at the Harbor Arts Gala and
$600 of raffle tickets and merchandise [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025].

## Contradictions

**What is the $4,500 gala table?**

- **The card analysis says charitable, in full.** Under version 2 of the standard any
  charge to a registered charity is charitable, so the analysis reports $9,400 of
  charitable spend including the whole table [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025].
- **The giving summary says $2,900 of gift and $1,600 of purchase.** The charity's
  acknowledgement values the dinner received at $1,600, which is not deductible, and
  the summary also excludes the $600 of raffle tickets and merchandise the card
  analysis had counted [^abernathy-ruiz-philanthropy-2025].
- **Version 3 of the standard says neither: it is "events & memberships".** From Q3
  2026 charity-related purchases go to a new category at the full amount, flagged
  `possible-charitable`, and only the giving summary states the deductible portion
  [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3].

The three positions are not reconciled in the library. The 2025 card analysis was
correct under the rules in force when it was produced and is not restated under
version 3, so the two 2025 numbers will continue to disagree
[^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. The client page carries both
[^synthesis]. See [[clients/abernathy-ruiz]].

## Why it matters beyond one table

Version 3 exists because the two teams' figures for the same client disagreed and
clients noticed [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. It also bars comparing
charitable or dining totals across versions without adjustment, which affects every
2026 card analysis that reports a year-on-year change
[^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. See
[[services/credit-card-spend-analysis]] and [[services/philanthropic-giving-summary]].

# Unused subscriptions

Every card analysis in the library has found recurring charges the household no longer
uses, and the finding scales with the number of subscriptions rather than with income
[^synthesis].

| client | recurring charges | unused | annual saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[clients/abernathy-ruiz]] | 47 | 9 | $2,340 [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025] |
| [[clients/kessler]] | 14 | 4 | $860 [^kessler-card-analysis-2025] |

The unused ones are of the same kinds in both households: duplicated streaming
services, memberships and plans that overlap with something else already paid for, and
tools or apps tied to an activity that has stopped [^abernathy-ruiz-card-analysis-2025]
[^kessler-card-analysis-2025].

## Definition

Version 3 of the categorisation standard fixes the definitions the 2025 analyses used
informally: a subscription is a charge of the same amount in three or more consecutive
months, and it is unused when there is no correlated activity for 90 days and the
client confirms it on review [^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3]. The annualised
saving from cancellation is a required output
[^firm-spend-categorisation-standard-v3].

## What is not yet known

Whether the cancellations happen: no follow-up analysis is in the library yet, so the
$2,340 and $860 are recommendations, not realised savings [^synthesis]. See
[[services/credit-card-spend-analysis]] and [[questions/open-questions]].
